summary.t: The most visible environmental problem is winter air pollution in Bishkek. In 2022 the city's annual mean PM2.5 was about 7 times the WHO guideline, and in winter daily means frequently exceed 200 µg/m³.
summary.h: The biggest environmental problem is Bishkek's winter air pollution

summary.t: The main cause is household coal heating. In winter months, residential heating accounts for up to nearly 40% of PM2.5, and 70% of homes nationwide are heated with coal.
summary.h: Household coal heating is the main cause

summary.t: National PM2.5 continues to fall but remains about 4 times the WHO guideline (5 µg/m³). The national target of "a 16% reduction in harmful emissions in Bishkek" cannot be measured because no emission figures are published.
summary.h: PM2.5 is falling but still about 4 times the WHO guideline

summary.t: Donor funding is concentrated on water, sanitation and waste facilities, while uranium tailings, hazardous substances and environmental governance have no active projects. Active cooperation aligned with the environmental management strategy totals 31 projects worth about USD 60.6 million.
summary.h: Funding concentrated on water, sanitation and waste; tailings and governance are gaps

summary.t: The EU's investment support for water, sanitation and waste (about USD 10.7 million) ends in late 2026. Its successor, and how NDP 2030's waste tasks (modern landfills, extended producer responsibility) are put into practice, will be the key issues for 2027.
summary.h: The successor to EU investment support is the key issue for 2027

sections.msg: There are four problems — air, sewerage, waste and legacy sites — and only air can be tracked with figures.

items.k: Bishkek PM2.5 relative to WHO guideline (2022)
Losses from air pollution as share of GDP (national)

paras.t: Air: the national annual mean PM2.5 fell from 36.1 µg/m³ (2010) to 20.6 µg/m³ (2023), but remains about 4 times the WHO guideline of 5 µg/m³. In urban areas it was 23.6 µg/m³ (2023).
paras.b: PM2.5 20.6 µg/m³ (2023), about 4 times the WHO guideline

paras.t: Bishkek: according to the World Bank, the city's annual mean PM2.5 in 2022 was about 7 times the WHO guideline, and in recent winters daily means have often exceeded 200 µg/m³. During the winter heating season, the city frequently ranks among the five most polluted cities in the world.
paras.b: Bishkek: about 7 times the WHO guideline; over 200 µg in winter

paras.t: [Academic study — not national statistics] A 2024 paper reports an annual mean PM2.5 of 48 µg/m³ at Bishkek monitoring sites in 2019–2021, winter daily means above 75 µg/m³ (peaking at 200 µg/m³), falling to around 10 µg/m³ in summer. These are estimates and observations from a paper, not national statistics.

Monitoring network: according to the UN in the Kyrgyz Republic's overview, there was only one automatic monitoring station in 2018. By 2024 this had grown to low-cost sensors (50 Clarity, 47 BlueSky, 24 AirKaz, 8 PurpleAir) and two reference stations (Kyrgyzhydromet and the US Embassy). Kyrgyzhydromet's long-standing network has 14 sites in 5 cities, 13 of which rely on manual sampling.

However, following the 2023 rules on registering producers of hydrometeorological data (Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 592), civil society groups removed sensors pending certification, and 7 more were removed during inspections. By February 2025, only 10 low-cost sensors remained on the public platform, and the number of operating Kyrgyzhydromet sensors had also fallen to 10.
Monitoring expanded sharply, but tighter regulation then thinned the publicly available data. The basis for verifying the effectiveness of air quality measures has, if anything, weakened.

Health and economy: in 2010–2019, air pollution caused about 4,100–5,000 premature deaths a year, equivalent to 12–13% of annual deaths. The World Bank estimates the cost of air pollution at 5.1% of GDP nationally and 1.2% for Bishkek alone.
paras.b: Premature deaths 4,100–5,000 a year; losses 5.1% of GDP

paras.t: The UNICEF report (2022) estimates the PM2.5 burden in Bishkek in July 2021–June 2022 at 112 deaths (95% confidence interval 97–131) and 3,568 disability-adjusted life years (DALYs, the healthy years lost to illness and premature death). Children bear 22% of the disease burden, and welfare losses amount to 2 billion som (USD 24.9 million).

Sewerage: according to the national water supply programme, 29.1% of the population has access to centralised sewerage (64.1% urban, under 10% rural), and the number of centralised sewerage systems fell from 117 (2013) to 96 (January 2018).
paras.b: Centralised sewerage 29.1%; number of systems falling

paras.t: Waste: there are only two figures for waste collection rates: Bishkek 83% (2010) and Osh 80% (2018). A new landfill for Bishkek is being developed under an EBRD project.
paras.b: Only two figures exist for waste collection rates

paras.t: According to the NDC (2021 update), greenhouse gas emissions in 2017 compared with 1990 fell by 55.53% in the energy sector but rose by 26.92% in the waste sector. The UN overview notes that there is still no national methodology for the air-related SDG indicators 3.9.1 and 11.6.2.

NDP 2030 Section 13.2 has four targets: expanding specially protected natural areas to 10% of the territory, reducing greenhouse gases by 16%, raising ND-GAIN (an index of climate resilience) by at least 3 points, and reducing harmful emissions in Bishkek by 16%. Only the last relates directly to environmental management.

Pollution of water sources: the national water supply programme states that many water sources are contaminated with nitrates, chromium, petroleum products and other substances because of settlement infrastructure, factories, agricultural and industrial waste, solid waste landfills, car washes and the lack of municipal drainage systems. Tackling waterborne diseases costs more than 4.8 billion som a year, with about 30,000 cases of acute intestinal infection annually.

The four problems are linked. Open burning of waste pollutes winter air, and the lack of sewerage pollutes water sources. Pursuing them through separate sectoral plans makes these links harder to see.

Only air can be tracked annually, through estimates by international organisations; sewerage, waste and tailings have no annual figures. The very basis for measuring progress in environmental management is weak.
paras.b: No annual figures other than for air

sections.msg: Environmental management policy is split into "NDP 2030 Section 13.2 (and 13.1) → Green Economy Development Programme 2025–29, the Bishkek city strategy, the water supply programme and the DRR action plan".

paras.t: Overarching plan: Section 13.2 of the National Development Programme 2030 sets as one of its targets "reducing harmful emissions in Bishkek by 16% through the use of enriched coal and the gasification of housing". Its tasks include gasification of housing in Bishkek and construction of coal enrichment plants at two sites, Kara-Keche and Min-Kush.
paras.b: NDP 2030 13.2: 16% reduction in harmful emissions in Bishkek

paras.t: Waste: Section 13.2 aims to reduce waste generation, promote reprocessing, reuse and safe disposal, introduce extended producer responsibility (under which manufacturers are responsible for products through to disposal) with digitalisation, build modern landfills meeting international standards and remediate unauthorised dumps.
paras.b: Waste: extended producer responsibility and modern landfills

paras.t: Environmental safety: Section 13.2 lists regulation of radiation safety, radioecological monitoring of former uranium sites, a chemicals register, disposal of obsolete pesticides and remediation of contaminated soil, and improved air quality monitoring. Section 13.1 sets the target of bringing 16 tailings ponds and waste dumps from the former uranium legacy into a safe condition.
paras.b: Uranium, chemicals and air monitoring

paras.t: Air quality institutions and plans

Air: the law on atmospheric air protection dates from 1999. The government plan (2021–2023) contained 43 measures and was revised in 2024 into a 32-item priority plan (2024–2025). An inter-ministerial commission chaired by the Minister of Natural Resources, Ecology and Technical Supervision has met more than 20 times, and Bishkek City Hall was delegated the ministry's air protection powers for two years from 1 January 2024.

According to the WHO case study, a Cabinet of Ministers order of 17 November 2021 established a temporary inter-ministerial commission chaired by the Mayor of Bishkek, with seven objectives including a study of health impacts, an air quality index and a phased improvement plan. The Ministry of Health's working group (December 2021) faced outdated disease reporting forms, shortages of staff and funding, and slow data collection.

Support for monitoring: according to the UN overview, ADB provided Kyrgyzhydromet with 50 Clarity sensors worth USD 90,000 in December 2020. The UNICEF report recommends coordinating measures through the inter-ministerial commission.
Waste and climate plans

As waste measures, the NDC cites systems for separate collection and disposal of waste, development of recycling, and biogas facilities at the Bishkek and Osh landfills. However, it does not estimate emission reductions because the investment is not secured. As the legal framework for climate and environment, it cites Presidential Decree No. 77 of 19 March 2021, "On measures to ensure environmental security and climate sustainability".

Sectoral plans: the site's gap table maps air to "Bishkek: Smart and Sustainable City" to 2033, water and sanitation to the Water Supply Programme 2026, waste and environmental governance to the Green Economy Development Programme 2025–2029, and tailings to the Action Plan for Emergency Risk Reduction 2025–2030.
paras.b: Separate plans cover each area

paras.t: Coordination of cooperation: the Air Quality Working Group of the Development Partners Coordination Council compiled an overview of clean air actions in 2018–2024, and in February 2025 the Ministry of Natural Resources, Ecology and Technical Supervision held a national dialogue with UNEP and the UN.
paras.b: Air quality coordinated through the partners' working group

paras.t: Environmental management has no single consolidated national programme; air, water, waste and tailings each fall under different plans. The texts of the Green Economy Development Programme and the Bishkek city strategy have not been read, and their targets have not been verified.
paras.b: No single consolidated national programme

paras.t: The delegation of air protection powers to Bishkek City Hall covers the two years from 2024 and expires at the end of 2025. Whether the powers are extended or returned will change the division of roles between city measures and national supervision.

sections.msg: Of the five areas, uranium tailings and hazardous substances, and environmental governance, have national targets but no active cooperation.

fig.cap: Table 1-1 Areas (active cooperation by matrix row; overlaps included)

paras.t: Five areas: air pollution; water, sanitation and wastewater treatment; waste and recycling; tailings, uranium and hazardous substances; environmental governance and impact assessment.
paras.b: Five areas

paras.t: NDP 2030's "16 uranium tailings sites" and "improved air quality monitoring" fall under the tailings and environmental governance areas respectively, but neither has any active cooperation. This is where the gap between targets and implementation is widest.
paras.b: Tailings and governance: targets exist, but no cooperation

paras.t: Of the bases for the five areas, the texts of the Green Economy Development Programme and the Bishkek city strategy could not be verified, so even though the table lists them as "in force", their targets are unknown. Only the water supply programme and the DRR action plan provide a basis with figures.

Of the five areas, water, sanitation and wastewater treatment largely overlaps with the projects in the water supply and sanitation rows of the water resources and water supply sector. Tailings, uranium and hazardous substances overlaps with technosphere safety in the DRR sector (Action Plan Chapter 3).
The five areas of environmental management lean on other sectors' plans. In practice, only air has targets and figures that can be tracked independently as an environmental area.

sections.h: Overall: prospects for national and international targets
sections.msg: Only PM2.5 can be tracked annually; it is on course for the WHO interim target but far from the guideline. National environmental targets cannot be measured.

fig.cap: Table 2-1 Gap to targets (actual pace = average change over the period; required pace = change needed to reach the target by 2030)

paras.t: No annual published figures can be found for NDP 2030's environmental management targets (16% reduction in harmful emissions in Bishkek, 16 uranium tailings sites). Only WHO-estimated PM2.5 can be tracked annually.
paras.b: National targets have no annual published figures

paras.t: National PM2.5 fell by −1.5 µg/m³/year in 2015–2023. At this pace, the WHO interim target (15 µg/m³) will be reached by 2030, but the guideline (5 µg/m³) requires −2.2 µg/m³/year and will not be met.
paras.b: On course for the 15 µg interim target; far from the 5 µg guideline

paras.t: National PM2.5 is a WHO population-weighted estimate, at a very different level from observations in Bishkek (annual mean 48 µg/m³, academic paper). Even if the national indicator falls, it cannot measure progress on NDP 2030's "16% reduction in harmful emissions in Bishkek".

The UN overview recommends aligning national air quality standards with the WHO guidelines with interim targets, extending measures to Osh, Jalal-Abad, Karakol and Talas, and having a plan for each city that exceeds the standards.

The same overview states that no single measure is sufficient: even by World Bank estimates, clean heating alone would reduce PM2.5 by only about 29%, and a full transition to zero-emission transport by only about 27%.

Because the national target is measured in "emissions" and the international indicator in "concentrations", the gap to the target cannot be shown in figures without an emissions inventory (how many tonnes come from where) linking the two. The UN overview also recommends building an emissions register.

Bishkek's annual mean varies slightly by source — the World Bank model (51.4 µg/m³, 2018), the paper's observations (48 µg/m³, 2019–21) and UNICEF's measurements (44 µg/m³, 2021–22) — but all are more than twice the national estimate (20.6 µg/m³) and about 9–10 times the WHO guideline.

sections.msg: National figures are falling, but Bishkek's winter levels are extremely high because of household coal heating.

fig.cap: Figure 2-1 Annual mean PM2.5 (national and urban; dotted line = WHO interim target of 15 µg/m³)

paras.t: Trends and background

paras.b: National 36.1 → 20.6; urban 40.8 → 23.6

paras.t: Variation within the city: the UNICEF report puts Bishkek's annual mean for July 2021–June 2022 at 44 µg/m³, with annual means by sensor ranging from 17 to 75 µg/m³, a fourfold spread, and the north the highest. The city average was 1.75 times that at the US Embassy monitoring site over the same period.

Gasification: according to the UN overview, 23,127 homes in 52 residential areas of Bishkek were connected to gas, and the city's gas contracts rose from 244,530 to 261,037 (2024). Residential gas use rose from 2.2 million m³ (2018) to 43 million m³ (2024), and coal use fell by 58,000 tonnes. By 2024, 93 public boilers had switched from coal to other energy sources.

Transport and waste: 1,292 new environmentally friendly buses were introduced (1,000 from the state budget, 120 from the city, 124 from EBRD and 48 from KfW), each replacing about 4 diesel minibuses. Fires at the Bishkek landfill were extinguished, which official estimates say reduced smog by 10–15%.

Enforcement: Bishkek city inspections checked 81,694 sites for prohibited burning, issuing 256 reports and 2,928,500 som in fines. Of 346 bathhouses and saunas, 245 used coal and 76 were closed. The Ministry of Natural Resources, Ecology and Technical Supervision carried out 1,002 inspections nationwide in 2024 and found 1,247 violations.
Sources of pollution

Sources: in the World Bank's analysis (2018 data), the largest contributors to the annual mean are residential heating, transport and windblown dust. In winter, residential heating is the largest, approaching 40% in some months. Transport is second in every season.
paras.b: Residential heating largest in winter; transport second

paras.t: Heating: about 40% of Bishkek's population uses individual heating; 98% of detached houses have individual heating, and 75% of those use coal as the main fuel. UNEP and UNDP suggest that the city's thermal power plant may contribute less than 1% of ground-level PM2.5.
paras.b: 75% of detached-house heating uses coal

paras.t: [Academic study — not national statistics] A 2024 paper (estimates from a paper, not national statistics) estimates contributions to Bishkek's annual mean PM2.5 as household cooking and heating 29%, transport 27%, transboundary inflows 21%, the combined heat and power plant 11% and dust 9%, with household heating reaching about 40% in January and November. City emissions total about 5,450 tonnes a year: transport 1,750 tonnes, housing 1,400 tonnes, dust 1,100 tonnes, industry 950 tonnes and open burning of waste 150 tonnes.

The World Bank's emissions inventory (2018) likewise puts Bishkek's PM2.5 emissions at 5,488.6 tonnes a year: transport 1,737.6 tonnes, residential heating 1,424.0 tonnes, urban dust 1,157.8 tonnes, combined heat and power and heat-only boilers 751.7 tonnes, industry 249.2 tonnes and open burning of waste 168.3 tonnes. There are 16 brick kilns around the city.
The World Bank recommends publishing data on the efficiency of the power plant's electrostatic precipitators and verifying them through independent regular audits.

The World Bank analysis and the paper agree that household heating and transport are the two main sources. However, methods produce different results for the power plant's contribution — UNEP and UNDP say it "may be less than 1%", while the paper puts it at 11%. The common conclusion is that no single measure is sufficient.
Power plant: Bishkek's combined heat and power plant was transferred to city management in 2024. Conversion to natural gas is planned, but funding has not yet been secured.

Heating methods: in UNICEF's survey, the main winter heating sources are district heating about 48%, coal stoves 26%, gas 17% and electricity 8%. Coal is used by 40% of the lowest-income group versus 17% of the highest. Compared with MICS 2018, gas rose by more than 12 points and coal fell by 14 points. Children in coal-burning homes have about 33% higher annual exposure than those in homes with district heating.

Coal heating is more common in lower-income households, and the harm from pollution falls heavily on children. Unless subsidies for heating conversion are designed to reach low-income households, both the reduction in pollution and its fairness will be limited.

Funding for conversion: according to the UN overview, a subsidised loan scheme of 1 billion som at 8% interest was set up for gas connections, but only 254 users borrowed, totalling just over 32 million som. There are 44 EV charging stations, 3,394 registered electric vehicles (early 2025) and 9 natural gas vehicle filling stations.

Effect of measures: if all coal-using households switched to clean heating, annual mean PM2.5 would fall by 29%, and switching the thermal power plant from coal to gas would reduce it by 9%. No single area alone achieves the required reduction.
paras.b: Heating conversion −29%; power plant gasification −9%

paras.t: Interpreting the gap to targets

Outlook: UNEP and UNDP project that under business as usual, PM2.5 emissions will increase by 60% by 2040, and recommend affordable alternatives to coal heating such as heat pumps, stricter fuel standards and a monitoring network using low-cost sensors.
paras.b: Under business as usual, emissions up 60% by 2040

paras.t: UN overview recommendations (heating): give early notice of a ban on coal heating from 2035 and provide subsidised finance for heat pumps and other alternatives. They also include grants for insulating old buildings, strict insulation and airtightness standards for new buildings, financing repaid from energy savings, a tax on coal and tax incentives for clean heating.

Recommendations (transport): collect data on vehicle types, model years and the presence of catalytic converters; raise average speeds with dedicated bus lanes; replace old diesel buses with gas or electric ones; ban the removal of catalytic converters; align standards with EU emission standards (EURO); and establish low-emission zones restricting traffic on high-pollution days.

UNICEF recommends designating coal-free zones, phasing out coal combined with affordable alternatives, a health-based air quality index, managing air quality across the whole airshed beyond city boundaries, and regular vehicle emission inspections (not currently carried out).

National measures (gasification of housing, coal enrichment) point in the same direction as "household heating conversion", which donor analyses consider most effective. However, the national target is measured in emissions, and no emission figures are published.
paras.b: Direction aligned; no figures to measure it

paras.t: World Bank estimates suggest full household heating conversion would cut concentrations by 29% and power plant gasification by 9%. Emissions and concentrations are not the same, but NDP 2030's "16% reduction" is within reach if heating conversion advances substantially. Conversely, it will be hard to achieve with gasification and coal enrichment alone if heating conversion stalls.
Link to donor projects

Related cooperation: the air row has 4 projects worth about USD 8.5 million, almost entirely the World Bank's air quality improvement project. The World Bank states that this analysis formed the basis for the USD 50 million project.
paras.b: Air about USD 8.5 million (mainly World Bank)

paras.t: The World Bank's air quality improvement project is a USD 50 million IDA credit (2024–2030), allocating USD 9.1 million to monitoring, USD 32.3 million to clean heating, USD 7.1 million to greening and USD 1.5 million to implementation support (UN overview). The site counts it as about USD 8.3 million after pro-rata allocation.

Other cooperation: ADB's electric urban transport (USD 50.65 million, 120 electric buses, 2022–2027), Korea's air quality improvement (USD 10 million, heat pumps and solar power for about 20 schools and kindergartens in Chui Region, 2025–2028), GIZ's heat pump demonstration (about USD 0.35 million) and Finland's monitoring modernisation (FINKMET I–III). The site counts the Korean project as about USD 0.2 million after pro-rata allocation.

Air quality cooperation channels funding into heating conversion, consistent with the measures the World Bank analysis considers most effective. On the other hand, the expansion of monitoring (at least 5 automatic stations per city and a laboratory for sensor calibration) and the emissions register recommended by the UN overview rely on parts of other projects, as the environmental governance row remains empty.

sections.msg: Sewerage and waste facilities are being developed, but there are no figures to measure results annually; tailings have neither funding nor figures.

paras.t: Sewerage
Sewerage: only 3% of rural homes, schools and health facilities are connected to sewerage, and 5 towns have no sewerage at all.
paras.b: Rural sewerage connection 3%

paras.t: The CAREC Institute report (2024) puts the share of people connected to centralised sewerage at 21% (78% in Bishkek, under 10% in the regions) and states that in remote towns and district centres it is falling by 1.5–2% a year as facilities deteriorate. The AIIB document states that rural areas have no centralised sewerage and wastewater is discharged untreated.
Impact on rivers: the UNECE water policy dialogue article lists untreated industrial and municipal wastewater, livestock, mining and illegal dumping near settlements as pressures on the Chu River.

Protecting Lake Issyk-Kul: the World Bank's second additional financing for rural water supply will design and build wastewater treatment and disposal systems for social facilities in Kurmentu and Ak-Bulak in Issyk-Kul Region to protect the lake.

The national water supply programme's indicator matrix also lists construction of wastewater treatment plants in two towns, Balykchy and Karakol, and improvement of wastewater treatment in Cholpon-Ata.

Wastewater treatment around Lake Issyk-Kul is better covered than in other regions, with overlapping cooperation from ADB's wastewater management (ended 2025), EBRD's Cholpon-Ata water project and the World Bank's treatment in two villages. By comparison, wastewater treatment in regional towns away from the lake appears thinly covered.
Waste
Waste: the only waste collection rate figures are Bishkek 83% (2010) and Osh 80% (2018), and the share treated is unknown.
paras.b: Only two data points for waste collection rates

paras.t: According to the UN overview, a textile waste incinerator with a capacity of up to 20 tonnes a day was installed in October 2023, and 1,160 garment factories signed formal waste management contracts. On 29 March 2024, a USD 95 million waste-to-energy investment agreement was signed.

UN overview recommendations (waste): extend collection to all settlements, including urban outskirts, to prevent open burning; make separation of metal, glass, plastic and paper mandatory; ban open burning of waste, including textiles, with penalties; convert organic waste into compost and biogas; ban single-use plastic plates and bags in public places so they are not used as fuel; and ventilation and fire prevention at landfills.

Emissions from open burning of waste (168.3 tonnes in the World Bank inventory) are about 3% of the total, but tend to occur on urban outskirts that collection does not reach. Extending collection addresses both waste and air pollution.

Major projects in the waste row: the EU's solid waste in Osh and Jalal-Abad (about USD 0.9 million, to December 2027), EBRD's Osh solid waste (about USD 0.4 million), ADB's preparation for environmental improvement in waste (about USD 0.3 million, 2025–2027) and Switzerland's hospital medical waste management (about USD 0.5 million).

Waste cooperation is concentrated in Osh and Jalal-Abad besides Bishkek; among the site's top projects, none targets waste collection and disposal in small and medium regional towns. Nor is there any project supporting the introduction of extended producer responsibility under NDP 2030.
Legacy sites and chemicals
Legacy sites: progress on works at the 16 tailings ponds and waste dumps from the former uranium legacy appears only in reports of the Ministry of Emergency Situations and donor project reports.
paras.b: Uranium tailings progress only in project reports

paras.t: Completed chemicals projects include reducing environmental risks from primary mercury mining at Khaidarkan (about USD 0.5 million, ended 2018), preventing releases of persistent organic pollutants (POPs) and mercury from improper handling of medical waste (about USD 0.7 million, ended 2018), and strengthening implementation of chemicals conventions (UNEP, about USD 0.1 million, ended 2025).

NDP 2030 Section 13.2 lists as tasks a chemicals inventory and national register, safe disposal of obsolete pesticides and remediation of contaminated soil, and improved regulation of radioactive materials and waste management.

Chapter 3 of the DRR Action Plan 2025–2030 provides for inter-ministerial working groups by area, such as hazardous production facilities, environmental and radiation monitoring and hydraulic structures (2025–2026), a concept for a technosphere monitoring system (2026), and proposals for a database of hazardous facilities and automated monitoring (2027–2028).

The site's materials state that progress on uranium tailings works appears in project reports of the EU, Russia and others, but in the site's project data the tailings, uranium and hazardous substances row has no active projects. It needs to be checked whether cooperation is missing from the data or whether this is a genuine gap.
Investment in facilities continues, but with no figures on collection rates, treatment rates or tailings remediation, it is impossible to verify whether investment has produced results.
paras.b: No figures to verify results

The tailings, uranium and hazardous substances row has none.

paras.t: Donor focus areas

Each donor's core projects: World Bank, additional financing for rural water supply (about USD 9 million), air quality improvement (about USD 8.3 million) and climate-resilient water services (about USD 8.3 million); EU, investment support for water supply and sanitation (three tranches) and solid waste in Osh and Jalal-Abad; EBRD, city-level water sub-projects such as Cholpon-Ata (about USD 7.2 million).

The about USD 10.7 million ending by late 2026 consists of the first and second tranches of the EU's investment support for water supply and sanitation (about USD 5.4 million and about USD 5.3 million). These two projects are also included in the waste row.

Of the about USD 60.6 million active, the water and sanitation row accounts for about USD 49.8 million, or 80%. Funding specific to environmental management is limited to air (about USD 8.5 million) and part of waste.

Coordination of air quality cooperation: the UN overview was compiled by the working group of the Development Partners Coordination Council with input from ADB, WHO, UNECE, the Climate and Clean Air Coalition (CCAC), IOM, UNEP, UNICEF, GIZ, the World Bank, Finland, KOICA, civil society and others.
Three projects worth about USD 10.7 million end by late 2026 (almost entirely the EU's investment support for water supply and sanitation).
paras.b: About USD 10.7 million ends by late 2026

paras.t: By area (by row, with overlaps): water and sanitation, 13 projects worth about USD 59.7 million; waste, 12 projects worth about USD 54.2 million (the EU's water, wastewater and solid waste project and ADB's Issyk-Kul wastewater management fall into both); tailings and hazardous substances, 3 projects worth about USD 1.3 million (e.g. Khaidarkan mercury mining, mercury and POPs from medical waste); environmental governance, 1 project worth about USD 1 million (national environmental monitoring and information management); air, 4 projects worth about USD 0.2 million.
paras.b: Mostly water, sanitation and waste; small amounts for tailings and governance

paras.t: Major completed projects: the EU's "Drinking Water, Wastewater and Solid Waste" (about USD 34 million, December 2025), ADB's Issyk-Kul wastewater management (about USD 11.8 million and about USD 6.4 million, June 2025), the World Bank's rural water supply (about USD 3.4 million) and national water resources management (about USD 2 million), and the EU's technical contract for solid waste in Osh (about USD 1.1 million, December 2024).

The single completed project in the environmental governance row strengthened institutional and legal capacity to improve the national environmental monitoring system and environmental information management (about USD 1 million, ended June 2019).

Small air quality projects: according to the UN overview, these included UNECE's emissions inventory work (about USD 50,000 each in 2018, 2020–21 and 2023), WHO training on the AirQ+ health risk assessment tool (30 experts, about USD 30,000, December 2023), and two IOM projects (awareness-raising and retrofitting of 12 homes, USD 600,000 in total, 2021–2025).

Until around 2023, air quality cooperation consisted mainly of small studies, training and awareness projects; the World Bank's air quality improvement project was the first to bring major funding to heating conversion.

Tailings and hazardous substances, and environmental governance, had small projects in the past but have no active projects now. Air had almost nothing in the past and has newly received funding through the World Bank project.
paras.b: Tailings and governance discontinued; air newly started

paras.t: Following its largest completed project, "Drinking Water, Wastewater and Solid Waste" (December 2025), the EU's first and second tranches of investment support for water supply and sanitation also end in December 2026. EU funding in environmental management will then centre on the third phase, which runs until 2030.

sections.msg: Two areas have no active cooperation: tailings, uranium and hazardous substances, and environmental governance and impact assessment.

fig.cap: Table 3-3 Strategy areas × donors (toggle between active, completed and cumulative)

paras.t: Areas with no active cooperation: tailings, uranium and hazardous substances; environmental governance and impact assessment.
paras.b: Gaps: tailings and hazardous substances; environmental governance

paras.t: The tailings and hazardous substances row has 0 active and 3 completed projects (about USD 1.3 million), and the environmental governance row 0 active and 1 completed (about USD 1 million). In both rows, cooperation since 2017 is limited to a few completed projects.

The environmental governance row is empty, yet the UN overview calls for a sensor calibration laboratory and a national reference laboratory, a real-time public data platform and an emissions register. The WHO case study also cites shortages of staff and data on the health side. This is an area where demand for technical cooperation exceeds demand for funding.

UN overview recommendations (health): national air quality standards in line with WHO recommendations, training for health workers in recording under the International Classification of Diseases (ICD-10), inclusion of air pollution as a risk factor for non-communicable diseases in national prevention plans, systematic collection of data on air pollution-related illness and death, and development of an air quality index.

The tailings and hazardous substances row has had no new projects since the mercury and POPs projects ended in 2018. No corresponding cooperation for NDP 2030's chemicals register and disposal of obsolete pesticides can be found in the site's data.

UNICEF also recommends household use of air purifiers during pregnancy and the first 1,000 days of life (e.g. lending through antenatal and postnatal care), reducing indoor tobacco smoke, and integrating air pollution into school curricula and teacher training.

No projects corresponding to indoor measures to protect children and pregnant women or to school-based learning can be found in the site's data. These could also be incorporated into health and education cooperation.

sections.msg: 2027 will test both the progress of heating conversion in Bishkek and the successors to water, sanitation and waste investment.

paras.t: For air, national measures (gasification, coal enrichment) and donor analyses (household heating conversion is most effective) are now aligned. The next step is whether emission and monitoring figures to measure progress can be published.
paras.b: Air: direction aligned; figures to measure it are the next step

paras.t: With the EU's investment support for water, sanitation and waste partly ending in late 2026, the question is who will fund NDP 2030's waste tasks (modern landfills, extended producer responsibility), and how.
paras.b: Waste: EU successor and putting national tasks into practice

paras.t: Uranium tailings and hazardous substances, and environmental governance, have national targets but no active cooperation. Technical cooperation on monitoring systems and registers is likely to be in greater demand than funding.
paras.b: Tailings and governance likely to call for technical cooperation

paras.t: The thinning of public air quality monitoring data affects the assessment of every measure. Whether certification arrangements for stations and sensors are put in place and data are published again is a precondition for verifying the effectiveness of measures in the 2026–2027 winter.

The UN overview's proposed "ban on coal heating from 2035" is a long-term target extending beyond the NDP 2030 period. How to connect it with national measures to 2030 (gasification, coal enrichment) will be an issue for the next national air quality plan.

In waste, the USD 95 million waste-to-energy investment agreement (March 2024) and the development of Bishkek's new landfill could significantly change waste treatment in Bishkek. The next checkpoints are construction progress and the expansion of collection to eliminate open burning.

To watch next quarter: Bishkek air quality readings during the winter heating season, implementation reports on the Green Economy Development Programme, EU successor projects, and reports on uranium tailings works.
paras.b: Winter air, green economy, EU successor and tailings
